subject: Physics
q: A ray strikes a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 35°. What is the angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray?
explanation: Angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 35°, both measured from the normal. The angle between the two rays is 35° + 35° = 70°.
misconception: 55° is the angle between the ray and the mirror surface, not between the two rays.
hints: Both angles are measured from the normal, not from the mirror.

subject: Physics
q: Two plane mirrors are placed at 60° to each other, with a candle between them. How many images of the candle are formed?
explanation: For mirrors inclined at angle θ, the number of images n = 360°/θ − 1 (when 360/θ is even). 360/60 − 1 = 5. This is the principle of the kaleidoscope.
misconception: 6 forgets to subtract 1: one of the “images” would coincide with the object itself.

subject: Physics
q: A girl 160 cm tall wants to see her whole body in a vertical plane mirror. What is the minimum length of mirror she needs?
options: It depends on how far she stands from the mirror
explanation: Light from her feet must reflect into her eyes at the mirror point halfway between her eye level and her feet; likewise for the top of her head. So the mirror need only be half her height, 80 cm, placed correctly — and this does not depend on her distance from the mirror.
misconception: Standing further back does not help: the image also moves further back by the same amount.
hints: Draw the ray from her toes to the mirror and into her eye.
Where on the mirror does that ray reflect, compared with her eye height?

subject: Physics
q: You walk straight towards a plane mirror at 2 m/s. At what speed does your image approach YOU?
explanation: The image is always as far behind the mirror as you are in front. If you move 2 m closer to the mirror in a second, the image also moves 2 m closer to the mirror from the other side, so the gap between you and your image shrinks by 4 m each second.
misconception: 2 m/s is the image’s speed relative to the mirror, not relative to you.
hints: How far is your image from you when you stand d metres from the mirror?
How fast does 2d change if d changes at 2 m/s?

subject: Physics
q: Where is the bulb placed in a torch that uses a concave mirror to produce a strong parallel beam?
options: Between the focus and the mirror
At the principal focus of the mirror
Far beyond the centre of curvature
explanation: Rays from a source at the focus of a concave mirror reflect parallel to the principal axis, producing a narrow, far-reaching beam. Car headlights and searchlights use the same arrangement.
hints: Rays parallel to the axis meet at the focus — reverse their direction.

subject: Physics
q: Why are convex mirrors used as rear-view mirrors in vehicles?
options: They are cheaper than plane mirrors.
They give a real image that can be focused.
They give a magnified image of following vehicles.
They always give an erect, diminished image and a wider field of view.
explanation: A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image. Because the image is smaller, a much wider area behind the vehicle fits in the mirror. (Vehicles therefore carry the warning that objects are closer than they appear.)
misconception: Convex mirrors never form real or magnified images.
hints: What kind of image does a convex mirror always form?

subject: Physics
q: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Where is the image formed?
options: 15 cm in front of the mirror (real)
7.5 cm in front of the mirror (real)
30 cm in front of the mirror (real)
explanation: Mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with u = −30 cm, f = −10 cm: 1/v = −1/10 + 1/30 = −2/30, so v = −15 cm. Negative v means the image is in front of the mirror and real. Sense check: the object is beyond C (20 cm), so the image lies between F and C.
misconception: 7.5 cm comes from adding the reciprocals instead of using the sign convention.
hints: Use 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with distances in front of the mirror negative.
The object is beyond the centre of curvature — where should the image lie?

subject: Physics
q: For the same concave mirror (f = 10 cm) with the object 30 cm away, the image forms 15 cm in front of the mirror. What is the magnification?
explanation: For mirrors m = −v/u = −(−15)/(−30) = −0.5. The negative sign means the image is inverted; |m| = 0.5 means half the object’s height — as expected for a real image of an object beyond C.
misconception: Real images formed by a single mirror are always inverted, so m must be negative.
hints: m = −v/u for mirrors.
Real images from a mirror are inverted — what sign does that give?

subject: Physics
q: Why does a well-cut diamond sparkle much more than a piece of glass of the same shape?
options: Diamond has a lower refractive index than glass.
Diamond’s very high refractive index gives a small critical angle (about 24°), so light is totally internally reflected many times before leaving.
Diamond absorbs all colours except white.
explanation: Total internal reflection happens when light inside a denser medium meets the surface at more than the critical angle. Diamond (n ≈ 2.42) has a critical angle of about 24°, compared with about 42° for glass, so light entering a cut diamond bounces around inside and emerges from the top in bright flashes, also split into colours.
hints: What condition is needed for total internal reflection?

subject: Physics
q: What is the critical angle for light going from glass (refractive index 1.5) into air?
explanation: At the critical angle the refracted ray grazes the surface (r = 90°): sin c = 1/n = 1/1.5 = 0.667, so c ≈ 41.8°. At incidence above 41.8°, light is totally internally reflected — the principle of optical fibres.
misconception: 48.2° is 90° − 41.8°, measured from the surface instead of the normal.
hints: At the critical angle the angle of refraction is 90°.
sin c = 1/n.

subject: Physics
q: A short-sighted (myopic) student cannot see the board clearly. Where is the image of the board formed in her eye, and which lens corrects it?
options: In front of the retina; a concave (diverging) lens
On the retina; no lens is needed
In front of the retina; a convex lens
Behind the retina; a convex lens
explanation: In myopia the eyeball is too long or the lens too strong, so rays from distant objects focus in front of the retina. A diverging lens spreads the rays slightly so they focus on the retina.
misconception: Convex lenses correct long-sightedness (hypermetropia), where the image falls behind the retina.
hints: Is the eye’s focusing too strong or too weak in myopia?

subject: Physics
q: A myopic person’s far point is 2 m away (they cannot see clearly beyond it). What power of spectacle lens do they need to see distant objects?
explanation: The lens must make rays from infinity appear to come from the far point, 2 m in front. So it is a diverging lens with f = −2 m, and P = 1/f = −0.5 D.
misconception: −2 D uses the far point in metres as the power instead of taking its reciprocal.
hints: The lens should form an image of a distant object at the far point.
P = 1/f with f in metres.

subject: Physics
q: We see the Sun about two minutes before it actually rises above the horizon, and for about two minutes after it has set. Why?
options: The Sun is larger than the Earth.
Light takes about 8 minutes to reach us.
Atmospheric refraction bends sunlight towards us around the curve of the Earth.
explanation: The atmosphere gets denser towards the ground, so its refractive index increases downwards and light from the Sun just below the horizon bends down towards an observer. This adds about 2 minutes to daylight at each end of the day and also flattens the setting Sun’s disc.
misconception: The 8-minute travel time applies all day long; it does not make sunrise early.
hints: How does the density of air change with height, and what does that do to light?

subject: Physics
q: White light passes through a glass prism and spreads into a spectrum. A second, identical prism is placed upside down just after the first. What emerges from the second prism?
explanation: Each colour is bent by a slightly different amount (violet most, red least) because the refractive index depends on wavelength. The inverted prism bends each colour back by exactly the same amount in the opposite direction, so the colours recombine into white light. Newton used this experiment to show that the colours are already present in white light and are not made by the prism.
misconception: Colours of light do not cancel to darkness; recombining them gives white.
hints: Why does the first prism separate the colours?
What does an inverted identical prism do to each colour’s deviation?

subject: Physics
q: A pinhole camera forms an image of a candle flame on its screen. What is the image like, and why?
options: Erect, because the pinhole acts as a lens
Inverted, because the pinhole reflects light
Erect and coloured, because of dispersion
Inverted, because light travels in straight lines through the pinhole
explanation: Rays from the top of the flame pass through the hole in straight lines and land low on the screen; rays from the bottom land high. So the image is inverted — evidence for the rectilinear propagation of light.
misconception: There is no lens in a pinhole camera; the inversion comes purely from straight-line travel.
hints: Trace a straight ray from the top of the flame through the hole.

subject: Physics
q: A swimming pool is 2 m deep. Looking straight down into it, how deep does it appear? (refractive index of water = 1.33)
explanation: Apparent depth = real depth ÷ refractive index = 2/1.33 ≈ 1.5 m. Light from the bottom bends away from the normal as it leaves the water, so it appears to come from a shallower point. Pools therefore look shallower than they are — a real safety hazard.
misconception: 2.66 m multiplies instead of dividing; the pool looks shallower, not deeper.
hints: When light leaves water, does it bend towards or away from the normal?
Apparent depth = real depth ÷ n.

subject: Physics
q: A current of 2 A flows through a bulb for 5 s. How much charge passes through it?
explanation: Q = I × t = 2 A × 5 s = 10 C. One ampere is one coulomb per second.
hints: Current is charge per second.

subject: Physics
q: The charge on one electron is 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. How many electrons make up a charge of 1 C?
explanation: n = Q/e = 1 / (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 6.25 × 10¹⁸ electrons. A current of 1 A means this many electrons pass a point every second.
hints: Divide the total charge by the charge on one electron.

subject: Physics
q: What current flows through a 60 W bulb working at its rated voltage of 220 V?
explanation: P = VI, so I = P/V = 60/220 ≈ 0.273 A. A higher-power bulb on the same supply draws proportionally more current.
misconception: 3.67 A divides the wrong way (V/P).
hints: P = V × I.

subject: Physics
q: A heater is rated 1000 W at 220 V. If it is connected to a 110 V supply (assume its resistance does not change), what power does it deliver?
explanation: Resistance is fixed: R = V²/P = 220²/1000 = 48.4 Ω. At 110 V, P = V²/R = 110²/48.4 = 250 W. Halving the voltage halves the current too, so power falls to a quarter.
misconception: 500 W assumes power is proportional to voltage; with fixed resistance it is proportional to V².
hints: What stays constant when the supply changes — power, current or resistance?
Use P = V²/R.

subject: Physics
q: A wire 2 m long with a cross-sectional area of 1 mm² has a resistance of 0.034 Ω. What is the resistivity of its material?
explanation: ρ = RA/L. 1 mm² = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m². ρ = 0.034 × 10⁻⁶ / 2 = 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m — the resistivity of copper, which is why copper is used for wiring.
misconception: 1.7 × 10⁻² Ω m forgets to convert mm² to m².
hints: Rearrange R = ρL/A.
1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m².

subject: Physics
q: A bird can perch safely on a single bare high-voltage power line. Why does it not get a shock?
options: Both its feet are at almost the same potential, so there is negligible potential difference across its body and almost no current flows through it.
High-voltage lines carry no current in the daytime.
The current in the wire is too small to hurt anything.
explanation: Current flows through a body only if there is a potential difference across it. The bird’s feet touch the same wire a few centimetres apart; the wire’s resistance over that distance is tiny, so the potential difference — and the current through the bird — is negligible. If the bird touched a second wire or the pole, a large potential difference would exist and the result would be fatal.
misconception: High voltage is dangerous only when there is a path between two very different potentials.
hints: What drives current through any conductor?

subject: Physics
q: In household wiring, where is the fuse connected, and why?
options: In the neutral wire, because it carries no current
In series in the live wire, so that when it melts the appliance is disconnected from the high potential
In the earth wire, so excess current flows to the ground
In parallel with the appliance, to share the current
explanation: A fuse is a thin wire of low melting point placed in series with the live wire. Excess current heats it until it melts, breaking the circuit and cutting off the live supply. If it were in the neutral wire, the appliance would stay connected to the live wire even after the fuse blew.
misconception: A fuse in parallel would not break the circuit at all.
hints: Which wire is at a high potential?

subject: Physics
q: Why are appliances with metal bodies, such as electric irons and washing machines, connected to an earth wire?
options: If a live wire touches the metal body, current flows safely to the ground instead of through the user.
To make the appliance use less electricity.
To make the appliance work faster.
To increase the voltage across the appliance.
explanation: The earth wire connects the metal body to the ground through a low-resistance path. If a fault makes the body live, a large current flows to earth, usually blowing the fuse or tripping the circuit breaker, and the body stays near zero potential, protecting the user.
hints: What would happen to someone touching a live metal body without an earth connection?

subject: Physics
q: Four identical 8 Ω resistors are first connected all in series, then all in parallel. What is the ratio of the series resistance to the parallel resistance?
explanation: Series: 4 × 8 = 32 Ω. Parallel: 8/4 = 2 Ω. Ratio = 32/2 = 16. In general, for n identical resistors the ratio is n².
misconception: 4 is the factor for one arrangement only; the effects multiply: ×4 in series and ÷4 in parallel.
hints: n identical resistors R: series nR, parallel R/n.
Divide one by the other.

subject: Physics
q: A student measures the current through a resistor at different voltages. What is its resistance?
explanation: V/I = 1.0/0.2 = 2.0/0.4 = … = 5 Ω for every reading, so the resistor obeys Ohm’s law: a V–I graph is a straight line through the origin.
misconception: 0.2 Ω is I/V, the inverse.
hints: R = V/I. Is it the same for every row?

subject: Physics
q: The current through a torch-bulb filament is measured as the voltage is increased. What do the data show?
options: The bulb is faulty, because current should double when voltage doubles.
The filament obeys Ohm’s law exactly.
The filament’s resistance increases as it gets hotter, so it does not obey Ohm’s law.
explanation: R = V/I: 2/0.40 = 5 Ω, 4/0.60 ≈ 6.7 Ω, 6/0.70 ≈ 8.6 Ω, 8/0.75 ≈ 10.7 Ω. As the voltage rises, the filament gets hotter and its resistance increases, so the current rises less and less. Ohm’s law holds only at constant temperature.
misconception: A non-linear V–I graph is not a fault; it shows resistance changing with temperature.
hints: Work out V/I for each column.
What happens to a filament’s temperature as more current flows?

subject: Physics
q: Five 100 W bulbs are used for 6 hours every day for 30 days. If electricity costs ₹6 per unit (kWh), what is the cost?
explanation: Energy = 5 × 0.1 kW × 6 h × 30 = 90 kWh. Cost = 90 × ₹6 = ₹540. Replacing them with 9 W LEDs would cost under ₹50 for the same light.
misconception: ₹90 is the number of units, not the cost.
hints: Total power in kW × hours = units (kWh).

subject: Physics
q: Why does switching on many high-power appliances at once in a home sometimes blow the main fuse?
options: Appliances are in parallel, so each one adds its current; the total current exceeds the fuse rating.
Appliances are in series, so the total resistance becomes too large.
Each new appliance raises the mains voltage.
More appliances make the wires colder.
explanation: In parallel, each appliance draws its own current (I = P/V) from the same supply, and the currents add up in the main wire. Too many at once can exceed the safe current, overheating the wiring; the fuse melts first to prevent a fire.
misconception: Adding resistances in parallel DECREASES the total resistance and increases total current.
hints: Are household appliances in series or parallel?
What happens to the total current when you add another branch?

subject: Physics
q: A 4 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor are connected in parallel across a 6 V battery. What is the total current drawn from the battery?
explanation: Each branch gets the full 6 V: I₁ = 6/4 = 1.5 A, I₂ = 6/12 = 0.5 A. Total = 2 A. (Check: combined resistance 4 × 12 / 16 = 3 Ω, and 6/3 = 2 A.) More current flows through the smaller resistor.
misconception: 0.375 A treats the resistors as in series (16 Ω).
hints: In parallel, each branch has the same voltage.
Add the branch currents.

subject: Physics
q: A current of 2 A flows through a 50 Ω heating element for 5 minutes. How much heat is produced?
explanation: Joule’s law: H = I²Rt = 2² × 50 × 300 s = 60,000 J = 60 kJ. Remember to convert minutes to seconds.
misconception: 1 kJ uses 5 s instead of 300 s.
hints: H = I²Rt with t in seconds.

subject: Physics
q: The north pole of a compass needle points towards the Earth’s geographic North. What kind of magnetic pole lies near the geographic North Pole?
explanation: Opposite poles attract. Since the compass’s north pole is attracted northwards, the Earth’s magnetic pole near the geographic North Pole must behave as a magnetic SOUTH pole.
hints: Do like poles or unlike poles attract?

subject: Physics
q: What is the shape of the magnetic field around a long straight wire carrying a current?
options: Straight lines parallel to the wire
There is no field around a straight wire
Straight lines pointing away from the wire
explanation: The field lines form circles centred on the wire, in planes perpendicular to it (Oersted’s discovery). Their direction is given by the right-hand thumb rule: thumb along the current, fingers curl in the direction of the field. The field is stronger closer to the wire.
hints: Imagine gripping the wire with your right hand.

subject: Physics
q: Why is a current-carrying solenoid with a soft-iron core used in electric bells and cranes, rather than a permanent magnet?
options: It is always stronger than every permanent magnet.
Its magnetism can be switched on and off and its strength controlled by the current.
explanation: An electromagnet is magnetic only while current flows, so a crane can drop its load by switching off, and a bell’s hammer can be pulled and released repeatedly. Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily, so the magnetism disappears when the current stops.
hints: What can you do with an electromagnet that you cannot do with a permanent magnet?

subject: Physics
q: A bar magnet is cut exactly in half across its middle. What do you get?
options: Two smaller magnets, each with its own north and south pole
One magnet and one non-magnetic piece
A separate north pole and a separate south pole
explanation: Magnetism comes from countless tiny aligned regions (domains) throughout the material, each itself a little magnet. Cutting the bar leaves aligned domains in both pieces, so new poles appear at the cut and each piece is a complete magnet. No isolated magnetic pole (monopole) has ever been observed.
misconception: The poles are not “stored” at the ends; every part of the magnet is magnetised.
hints: Where does a magnet’s magnetism come from — the ends or the whole bar?
What would you expect at the cut surfaces?

subject: Physics
q: In a simple DC electric motor, what is the job of the split-ring commutator?
options: To increase the voltage of the battery
To make the magnetic field stronger
To reverse the current in the coil every half turn so that it keeps rotating in the same direction
To convert DC into AC for the supply
explanation: After half a turn, the forces on the coil would start to push it back. The commutator reverses the coil’s current at that moment, reversing the forces, so the coil continues to turn the same way.
hints: What would happen to the coil after half a turn if the current did not change direction?

subject: Physics
q: In an AC generator, a coil rotates in a magnetic field. Why does the current it produces alternate in direction?
options: Each side of the coil moves up through the field and then down through it in every rotation, so the induced current reverses each half turn.
explanation: The direction of induced current depends on the direction of motion relative to the field (Fleming’s right-hand rule). Each half rotation, each side of the coil changes from moving up to moving down, so the current reverses. India’s mains supply alternates at 50 Hz.
hints: Follow one side of the coil through a whole rotation.

subject: Physics
q: Why does a transformer work with alternating current (AC) but not with steady direct current (DC)?
options: A voltage is induced in the secondary coil only when the magnetic field through it changes, and only AC produces a continually changing field.
AC has a higher voltage than DC.
DC flows only in the secondary coil.
DC is too weak to magnetise iron.
explanation: Electromagnetic induction needs a changing magnetic flux. AC in the primary coil makes the iron core’s magnetism grow, shrink and reverse continuously, inducing an AC voltage in the secondary. Steady DC gives a constant field, so (apart from a brief pulse when switched on) nothing is induced.
hints: What must be happening to the magnetic field for induction to occur?

subject: Physics
q: An ideal transformer steps 220 V down to 11 V for a doorbell. If the primary coil has 2000 turns, how many turns does the secondary coil have?
explanation: For an ideal transformer Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, so Ns = 2000 × 11/220 = 100 turns. A step-down transformer has fewer secondary turns.
misconception: 40,000 assumes a step-up transformer.
hints: Voltage ratio = turns ratio.

subject: Physics
q: Iron filings sprinkled around a bar magnet are packed most densely near the ends of the magnet. What does this show?
options: The magnet is weakest at its ends.
The magnetic field is strongest near the poles.
Iron filings are attracted only by north poles.
The magnet has no field in the middle.
explanation: The density of field lines (and filings) represents field strength. Lines crowd together near the poles, where the field is strongest, and spread out further away. The field is weak — but not zero — around the middle.
hints: What does the closeness of field lines represent?

subject: Physics
q: A strong magnet is dropped down a vertical copper pipe. It falls much more slowly than an identical non-magnetised piece of metal, even though copper is not attracted to magnets. Why?
options: Air resistance is greater for magnets.
The moving magnet induces currents in the copper, and these currents produce a magnetic field that opposes the magnet’s motion.
The magnet becomes lighter inside the pipe.
Copper becomes magnetic and attracts the magnet.
explanation: As the magnet falls, the magnetic flux through each ring of the pipe changes, inducing circulating (eddy) currents. By Lenz’s law, these currents create a field that opposes the change causing them — slowing the magnet. The magnet’s lost energy heats the pipe slightly. Magnetic braking in trains uses this effect.
misconception: Copper is not attracted to a stationary magnet; the effect exists only because the magnet is moving.
hints: What happens in a conductor when the magnetic field through it changes?
In which direction do induced effects act — helping or opposing the change?

subject: Physics
q: Which set contains only materials that are strongly attracted by a magnet?
explanation: Iron, nickel, cobalt and their alloys such as most steels are ferromagnetic: their domains line up with an external field, so they are strongly attracted. Copper, aluminium, gold, silver and brass are not.
misconception: Not all metals are magnetic.
hints: Coins and drink cans are metal — are they attracted?

subject: Physics
q: Maglev trains float a few centimetres above the guideway using magnets. What is the main physical advantage?
options: They make the Earth’s gravity weaker.
They need no energy at all to move.
They are unaffected by air resistance.
There is no contact friction with the track, so very high speeds are possible with less wear.
explanation: Magnetic repulsion (or attraction) lifts the train, removing wheel–rail friction and rolling resistance, and changing magnetic fields push it along. Maglev trains have exceeded 600 km/h. Air resistance still acts, and energy is still needed for propulsion and to overcome drag.
hints: Which force on a normal train is removed by levitation?

subject: Physics
q: A steel spoon and a wooden spoon have been in the same drawer all night. The steel one feels colder to touch. Why?
options: Steel absorbs cold from the air.
The steel spoon is at a lower temperature.
Steel conducts heat away from your hand faster, although both are at the same temperature.
explanation: Both spoons are at room temperature. Your skin senses the rate at which heat leaves it. Steel is a good conductor, so it draws heat rapidly from your warmer hand, which feels cold; wood is an insulator, so little heat flows.
misconception: “Cold” is not a substance that flows; what you feel is heat leaving your skin.
hints: Are the two spoons at different temperatures?

subject: Physics
q: Why does a sea breeze blow from the sea towards the land on a sunny afternoon?
options: Land heats up faster than water, so warm air rises over the land and cooler air from over the sea moves in to replace it.
Waves push the air towards the land.
The sea is warmer than the land in the afternoon.
explanation: Water has a much higher specific heat capacity than soil and rock, so in sunlight the land warms faster. Air above the land expands, becomes less dense and rises (convection); cooler, denser air from over the sea flows in. At night the land cools faster and a land breeze blows out to sea.
hints: Which warms up faster in sunshine: land or water?
What does warm air do?

subject: Physics
q: A 500 g block of metal at 100 °C is dropped into 500 g of water at 20 °C in an insulated container. The final temperature is 24 °C. What is the specific heat capacity of the metal? (water: 4200 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹)
explanation: Heat gained by water = 0.5 × 4200 × (24 − 20) = 8400 J = heat lost by metal = 0.5 × c × (100 − 24). So c = 8400 / 38 ≈ 221 J kg⁻¹ °C⁻¹. The water’s temperature changes little because its specific heat is about 19 times larger.
misconception: 840 uses the metal’s temperature change as 20 °C; it fell by 76 °C.
hints: Heat lost by the metal = heat gained by the water.
The metal cooled from 100 °C to 24 °C.

subject: Physics
q: Why are solar water heaters and solar cookers painted black?
options: Black surfaces lose no heat at all.
Black surfaces absorb most of the radiation falling on them.
Black surfaces reflect heat back to the Sun.
explanation: Dull black surfaces are the best absorbers of radiant energy (and also the best emitters). Shiny or white surfaces reflect most radiation. Solar cookers often add a glass cover to trap the heat (a mini greenhouse effect).
hints: Which colour feels hottest to wear in summer sunshine?

subject: Physics
q: In winter, a lake freezes over, yet fish survive in liquid water at the bottom. What property of water makes this possible?
options: Ice is denser than water and sinks, warming the surface.
Fish produce enough heat to keep the lake liquid.
Water at the bottom is under too much pressure to freeze at any temperature.
Water is densest at about 4 °C, so the coldest water and ice stay at the top while the bottom stays near 4 °C.
explanation: Most liquids contract steadily on cooling, but water contracts only down to 4 °C and then expands as it cools further (anomalous expansion). Water below 4 °C is less dense, so it stays on top and freezes at the surface. Ice is lighter still and floats, insulating the water beneath, which remains liquid at about 4 °C.
misconception: If ice sank, lakes would freeze solid from the bottom up.
hints: At what temperature is water densest?
Where does less-dense water go?

subject: Physics
q: Double-glazed windows (two panes with a gap) keep rooms warmer in winter mainly because:
options: the second pane absorbs the cold
glass is a very good insulator by itself
the trapped layer of air or gas between the panes is a poor conductor of heat
two panes of glass reflect all the heat back
explanation: Gases are very poor conductors. A thin sealed gap is too narrow for much convection, so heat flow by conduction through the window is greatly reduced. Woollen clothes and fur work the same way, by trapping air.
hints: What is between the two panes?

subject: Physics
q: A clinical thermometer usually reads from about 35 °C to 42 °C. Why is its range so narrow?
options: Human body temperature stays within this range, and a narrow range allows finer, more precise readings.
It is cheaper to print fewer numbers.
explanation: Body temperature (normal about 37 °C) rarely goes outside 35–42 °C even in illness. Spreading this small range along the whole tube makes each tenth of a degree visible. A laboratory thermometer covers a wider range (e.g. −10 °C to 110 °C) with less precision.
misconception: Mercury freezes at −39 °C, far below 35 °C.
hints: What is the thermometer designed to measure?

subject: Physics
q: Normal human body temperature is 37 °C. What is this on the Fahrenheit scale?
misconception: 66.6 °F forgets to add 32; 310 is the Kelvin value (≈ 310 K).

subject: Physics
q: Rain falls vertically at 4 m/s. A man walks through it at 3 m/s. At what speed does the rain hit him, relative to himself?
explanation: Relative to the man, the rain has his velocity subtracted: 4 m/s downward plus 3 m/s towards him (horizontally). These are perpendicular, so the relative speed is √(3² + 4²) = 5 m/s. That is why he tilts his umbrella forward.
misconception: 7 m/s simply adds the speeds; perpendicular velocities combine by Pythagoras.
hints: Velocities at right angles combine like the sides of a right-angled triangle.

subject: Physics
q: A boat heads straight across a 100 m wide river at 5 m/s relative to the water. The river flows at 3 m/s. How far downstream of the starting point does it land on the opposite bank?
explanation: The crossing motion and the drift are independent. Time to cross = 100 m ÷ 5 m/s = 20 s, during which the current carries the boat 3 × 20 = 60 m downstream. (Its speed relative to the bank is √(5² + 3²) ≈ 5.8 m/s, but that is not needed.)
misconception: 33 m divides 100 by 3. The time comes only from the across-river speed.
hints: How long does it take to cross, using only the across-river velocity?
How far does the current carry it in that time?

subject: Physics
q: A ball is thrown vertically upward at 20 m/s. What maximum height does it reach? (g = 10 m/s², no air resistance)
explanation: At the top v = 0. v² = u² − 2gh → 0 = 400 − 20h → h = 20 m.
misconception: 40 m forgets the factor of 2 in 2gh.
hints: At the highest point the velocity is zero.
Use v² = u² − 2gh.

subject: Physics
q: A ball thrown straight up returns to the thrower’s hand 6 s later. With what speed was it thrown? (g = 10 m/s²)
explanation: Without air resistance the motion is symmetric: 3 s up and 3 s down. Going up, its speed falls by 10 m/s every second to zero after 3 s, so u = 10 × 3 = 30 m/s.
misconception: 60 m/s uses the whole 6 s for the upward journey.
hints: How long does the upward part of the flight take?

subject: Physics
q:
A ball is thrown up and caught at the same height. For the whole flight:
I. Its displacement is zero.
II. The distance it travels is zero.
III. Its average velocity is zero.
IV. Its acceleration is zero at the top.
Which are correct?
explanation: It ends where it started, so displacement and average velocity are zero (I, III). It certainly travelled a distance — up and down (II false). Acceleration is g downward throughout, including at the top where the velocity is momentarily zero (IV false).
hints: Which quantities depend on direction and which only on path length?

subject: Physics
q: What does a straight, sloping line on a distance–time graph show?
explanation: A straight line has a constant slope, and the slope of a distance–time graph is speed. So the object covers equal distances in equal times — uniform motion. A horizontal line means rest; a curve means changing speed.
hints: What does a constant slope mean on this graph?

subject: Physics
q: A car travels for the first half of its journey TIME at 40 km/h and for the second half of the TIME at 60 km/h. What is its average speed?
explanation: With equal times t at each speed: distance = 40t + 60t = 100t in time 2t, so the average is 50 km/h. (If instead each HALF THE DISTANCE were at 40 and 60 km/h, the answer would be 48 km/h, because more time is spent at the lower speed.)
misconception: 48 km/h is the answer for equal distances, not equal times.
hints: Let each half of the time be t hours. How far does it go in each half?
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.

subject: Physics
q: A stone on a string is whirled in a horizontal circle of radius 2 m, completing one revolution every 4 s. What is its speed?
explanation: Distance per revolution = circumference = 2πr = 2π × 2 ≈ 12.57 m. Speed = 12.57/4 ≈ 3.14 m/s.
misconception: 12.6 m/s forgets to divide by the 4 s period.
hints: How far does the stone travel in one revolution?

subject: Physics
q: A 10,000 kg truck moves at 1 m/s and a 1000 kg car moves at 10 m/s. Which has more momentum?
options: It cannot be decided without knowing the direction.
explanation: Momentum p = mv: truck 10,000 × 1 = 10,000 kg m/s; car 1000 × 10 = 10,000 kg m/s. They are equal in size. (The car has ten times the kinetic energy, though: KE = ½mv².)
misconception: A huge mass is not enough; momentum depends on mass AND velocity.
hints: Calculate m × v for each.

subject: Physics
q: A 2 kg trolley moving at 3 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg trolley, and they stick together. What is their common velocity just after the collision?
explanation: Momentum is conserved: 2 × 3 + 1 × 0 = (2 + 1) × v → v = 6/3 = 2 m/s. Kinetic energy is NOT conserved here (9 J before, 6 J after); the rest becomes heat and sound.
misconception: 1.5 m/s divides the momentum by 4 instead of the combined mass of 3 kg.
hints: What is the total momentum before the collision?
After sticking, what mass moves together?

subject: Physics
q: Why do seat belts reduce injuries when a car stops suddenly?
options: They stop the passenger continuing forward because of inertia, and spread the stopping force over the body.
They make the car stop more slowly.
They push the passenger backwards with a reaction force.
explanation: When the car stops, the passenger’s body tends to keep moving forward (Newton’s first law). The belt applies the stopping force across the strong chest and pelvis and stretches slightly, increasing the stopping time, instead of the body hitting the dashboard or windscreen.
hints: What does an unrestrained body do when the car suddenly stops?

subject: Physics
q: A girl stands on a weighing scale in a lift. The lift cable snaps and the lift falls freely. What does the scale read during the fall?
explanation: In free fall she and the scale both accelerate downward at g. The scale does not need to push on her at all: N − mg = −mg gives N = 0. She is still pulled by gravity — she feels weightless because nothing supports her. Astronauts in orbit experience the same thing.
misconception: Gravity has not disappeared; the scale reads the supporting force, which becomes zero.
hints: What does a weighing scale actually measure?
Write F = ma for the girl with a = g downward.

subject: Physics
q: A 2 kg ball at rest is kicked with an average force of 50 N lasting 0.2 s. With what speed does it leave the foot?
explanation: Impulse = F × t = 50 × 0.2 = 10 N s = change in momentum. v = 10/2 = 5 m/s.
hints: Impulse = force × time = change in momentum.

subject: Physics
q: One newton is the force that:
options: gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s²
explanation: From F = ma: 1 N = 1 kg × 1 m/s² = 1 kg m s⁻². The weight of 1 kg on Earth is about 9.8 N, not 1 N.
misconception: Moving at constant velocity needs no net force at all.
hints: Use F = ma.

subject: Physics
q: A 10 kg crate is pushed across a floor at constant velocity by a horizontal force of 30 N. What is the coefficient of friction between the crate and the floor? (g = 10 m/s²)
explanation: Constant velocity means zero net force, so friction = 30 N. Friction = μ × normal force = μ × mg, so μ = 30/(10 × 10) = 0.3.
misconception: If the crate moves at constant velocity, the push does not exceed friction — it equals it.
hints: At constant velocity, what is the net force?
Friction = μ × normal force.

subject: Physics
q: A planet has one-quarter of Earth’s mass and half of Earth’s radius. How does the acceleration due to gravity on its surface compare with Earth’s?
explanation: g = GM/R². Mass × ¼ multiplies g by ¼; radius × ½ multiplies g by 1/(½)² = 4. Together ¼ × 4 = 1, so g is unchanged.
misconception: A smaller mass does not necessarily mean weaker surface gravity — being closer to the centre matters too.
hints: Write g = GM/R² and apply both changes.

subject: Physics
q: The Moon is pulled towards Earth by gravity. Why does it not crash into Earth?
options: The Moon’s own gravity pushes Earth away.
The Sun’s gravity cancels Earth’s pull.
It is falling towards Earth all the time, but its sideways speed carries it forward so it keeps missing Earth.
The Moon is too far away for gravity to act.
explanation: Gravity provides the centripetal force that bends the Moon’s path into a circle. Without gravity it would fly off in a straight line; with gravity but no sideways speed it would fall straight in. With both, it falls continuously around Earth — Newton’s insight that the apple and the Moon obey the same law.
misconception: Gravity acts at any distance; it weakens but never switches off.
hints: What would the Moon do if gravity suddenly vanished?
What would it do if its sideways motion stopped?

subject: Physics
q: What mainly causes ocean tides on Earth?
options: Heating of the oceans by the Sun
The difference in the Moon’s gravitational pull on the near and far sides of Earth
explanation: The Moon pulls the near side of Earth more strongly than its centre, and its centre more strongly than the far side. This stretching creates two bulges of water, and Earth rotates through them, giving about two high tides a day. The Sun has a smaller effect; when aligned with the Moon it produces larger spring tides.
hints: Gravity weakens with distance — does it pull equally on all parts of Earth?

subject: Physics
q: What is the gravitational force between two 1000 kg lead spheres whose centres are 1 m apart? (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
explanation: F = Gm₁m₂/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 10³ × 10³ / 1² = 6.67 × 10⁻⁵ N — about the weight of a grain of sand. Gravity between everyday objects is tiny, which is why Cavendish needed a delicate torsion balance to measure G.
hints: Multiply the masses: 10³ × 10³ = 10⁶.

subject: Physics
q: A flat sheet of paper and a stone are dropped together; the stone lands first. The same paper crumpled into a tight ball falls almost as fast as the stone. What does this show?
options: Crumpling the paper makes it heavier.
Gravity pulls harder on crumpled paper.
The difference was caused by air resistance, which depends on shape and area, not by gravity.
explanation: The paper’s mass is unchanged by crumpling, so its weight is unchanged. What changes is its area facing the air, and therefore the air resistance. Gravity accelerates both objects equally; air resistance is what slows the flat sheet.
hints: What changed when the paper was crumpled — its mass or its shape?

subject: Physics
q: Suppose Earth shrank to half its present radius while keeping the same mass. What would happen to your weight standing on its surface?
options: It would not change, because the mass is the same.
It would become four times as large.
explanation: g = GM/R². With M unchanged and R halved, g becomes GM/(R/2)² = 4GM/R², four times larger. You would be twice as close to Earth’s centre, and gravity follows an inverse-square law.
misconception: Surface gravity depends on the radius as well as the mass.
hints: How does g depend on R?
What is 1/(½)²?

subject: Physics
q: A porter lifts a 5 kg box 2 m onto his head, then walks 10 m along a level platform at constant speed. How much work does he do on the box against gravity in total? (g = 10 m/s²)
explanation: Lifting: W = mgh = 5 × 10 × 2 = 100 J. Walking horizontally at constant speed: the supporting force is vertical while the displacement is horizontal, so (ideally) no further work is done on the box against gravity. Total = 100 J.
misconception: 600 J adds 5 × 10 × 10 for the horizontal walk, but the force and displacement are perpendicular there.
hints: Work = force × displacement in the direction of the force.
In which direction does the porter push on the box while walking?

subject: Physics
q: A roller-coaster car starts from rest at the top of a 45 m high track. Ignoring friction, how fast is it moving when it reaches a point 25 m above the ground? (g = 10 m/s²)
explanation: Only the height DROPPED matters: 45 − 25 = 20 m. mgΔh = ½mv² → v = √(2 × 10 × 20) = √400 = 20 m/s. The shape of the track in between makes no difference.
misconception: 30 m/s uses the full 45 m drop; 22.4 m/s uses 25 m.
hints: How much height has the car lost?
Lost PE = gained KE.

subject: Physics
q: A car’s engine provides a driving force of 2000 N while the car moves at a steady 25 m/s. What power is the engine delivering?
hints: Power = force × velocity.

subject: Physics
q: Two bodies of mass 1 kg and 4 kg have the same kinetic energy. What is the ratio of their momenta (1 kg : 4 kg)?
explanation: KE = p²/2m, so p = √(2m × KE). With equal KE, p ∝ √m: √1 : √4 = 1 : 2. Check: if KE = 8 J, the 1 kg body moves at 4 m/s (p = 4) and the 4 kg body at 2 m/s (p = 8).
misconception: 1 : 4 assumes momentum is proportional to mass; with equal KE the heavier body moves more slowly.
hints: Express kinetic energy in terms of momentum.
Try a number: pick a KE and find each speed.

subject: Physics
q: Which energy changes take place in a filament bulb that is switched on?
explanation: Electric current heats the filament until it glows, so electrical energy becomes heat and light. Most of it becomes heat, which is why filament bulbs are inefficient.
hints: What is supplied to the bulb, and what does it give out?

subject: Physics
q: Loading a heavy drum onto a truck by rolling it up a long sloping plank, rather than lifting it straight up, mainly:
options: increases the drum’s potential energy at the top
reduces the work needed to the same height
reduces the force needed, though (without friction) the work done is the same
removes the need to do any work
explanation: The gain in potential energy (mgh) is the same either way. On a ramp the force is applied over a longer distance, so a smaller force is needed: F × ramp length = mgh. Friction actually makes the ramp require slightly more total work.
misconception: Simple machines trade force for distance; they cannot reduce the work below mgh.
hints: Is the final height of the drum the same either way?

subject: Physics
q: A 50 kg student runs up a 3 m high staircase in 5 s; her friend of the same mass walks up in 15 s. What power does the runner develop, and how does the work done by each compare? (g = 10 m/s²)
options: 100 W; both do the same work
1500 W; the walker does more work
300 W; the runner does three times more work
300 W; both do the same work
explanation: Work = mgh = 50 × 10 × 3 = 1500 J for both. Power = work/time: runner 1500/5 = 300 W, walker 1500/15 = 100 W. Running feels harder because the body must deliver energy three times faster.
misconception: Doing the same task faster needs more power, not more work.
hints: Does the work depend on how fast they climb?
Power = work ÷ time.

subject: Physics
q: A girl’s voice usually has a higher pitch than a man’s. Which property of the sound wave decides pitch?
explanation: Pitch is our perception of frequency: higher frequency, higher pitch. Amplitude decides loudness. In air all sounds travel at the same speed.
misconception: A loud sound is not necessarily high-pitched; loudness and pitch are different properties.
hints: Which property measures vibrations per second?

subject: Physics
q: The highest frequency most young people can hear is about 20 kHz. What is the wavelength of this sound in air (speed 340 m/s)?
explanation: λ = v/f = 340/20,000 = 0.017 m = 1.7 cm. At the lowest audible frequency, 20 Hz, λ = 17 m.
misconception: 17 m is the wavelength at 20 Hz, the LOWEST audible frequency.
hints: λ = v/f with f = 20,000 Hz.

subject: Physics
q: As an ambulance with its siren on drives towards you, the siren sounds higher-pitched; as it moves away, lower. Why?
options: Its motion squashes the sound waves ahead of it (shorter wavelength, higher frequency) and stretches those behind.
Sound travels faster from a moving source.
The driver changes the siren’s pitch.
Wind from the ambulance changes the pitch.
explanation: This is the Doppler effect. Each wave crest is emitted from a point slightly closer to you than the last, so the crests arrive closer together — a higher frequency. Behind the ambulance they are spread out. The speed of sound in the air is unchanged. Astronomers use the same effect with light (redshift).
misconception: The speed of sound in air does not depend on the speed of the source.
hints: Think about where each new wave crest is emitted from.
Crests closer together means what frequency?

subject: Physics
q: Why are the walls and ceilings of auditoriums often covered with soft, porous materials such as fibreboard and heavy curtains?
options: To increase the speed of sound
To absorb sound and reduce reverberation (repeated echoes)
To reflect more sound towards the stage
explanation: In a large hall with hard walls, sound reflects many times and persists (reverberation), making speech blurred. Soft porous materials absorb sound energy, cutting reverberation to a comfortable level. Curved ceilings may also be shaped to spread sound evenly.
hints: What happens to sound that hits a hard wall compared with a soft curtain?

subject: Physics
q: You see a lightning flash and hear the thunder 3 seconds later. Roughly how far away was the lightning? (speed of sound = 340 m/s)
explanation: Light arrives almost instantly, so the 3 s delay is the sound’s travel time: d = 340 × 3 = 1020 m, about 1 km. (A handy rule: about 3 seconds per kilometre.) There is no echo here, so no halving.
hints: Light takes almost no time to arrive, so the delay is due to sound.

subject: Physics
q: How does the speed of sound in air change as the air temperature increases?
explanation: In warmer air the molecules move faster and pass on vibrations more quickly. Sound travels at about 331 m/s at 0 °C, rising by about 0.6 m/s for each 1 °C (≈ 343 m/s at 20 °C).
hints: How fast do air molecules move in warmer air?

subject: Physics
q: In a hydraulic lift, a force of 50 N is applied to a small piston of area 2 cm². What force acts on the large piston of area 100 cm²?
explanation: Pascal’s law: pressure is transmitted equally through the liquid. P = 50/2 = 25 N per cm². Force on the large piston = 25 × 100 = 2500 N. The small piston must move 50 times further, so no energy is gained.
misconception: 1 N inverts the area ratio.
hints: The pressure is the same on both pistons.

subject: Physics
q: Why is the wall of a dam built much thicker at the bottom than at the top?
options: Because the top must let water overflow.
Water pressure increases with depth, so the force on the lower part of the wall is greatest.
To make it easier to build.
The water at the bottom is heavier.
explanation: P = hρg grows with depth h, so the push on each square metre of wall is greatest near the bottom. A thicker base resists this larger force. The pressure depends on the depth, not on how much water is stored behind the dam.
hints: How does liquid pressure depend on depth?

subject: Physics
q: When you suck on a straw, juice rises into your mouth. What actually pushes the juice up?
options: Your mouth pulling the juice up
Atmospheric pressure on the juice surface, which is greater than the reduced pressure inside the straw
explanation: Sucking lowers the air pressure inside the straw. The atmosphere (about 1 × 10⁵ Pa) presses on the juice in the glass and pushes it up the straw. On the Moon, with no atmosphere, a straw would not work.
misconception: Suction does not pull; the higher outside pressure pushes.
hints: What is pressing on the surface of the juice in the glass?

subject: Physics
q: A submarine is 200 m below the sea surface. What is the pressure due to the sea water alone? (density of sea water = 1030 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s²)
explanation: P = hρg = 200 × 1030 × 10 = 2.06 × 10⁶ Pa — about 20 times atmospheric pressure, pushing on every square metre of the hull with over 2 million newtons.
hints: P = hρg.

subject: Physics
q: Why does a hot-air balloon rise when the burner heats the air inside it?
options: Heat reduces the mass of the basket.
Hot air is pulled upward by the Sun.
Heated air expands and becomes less dense than the cooler outside air, so the buoyant force exceeds the balloon’s total weight.
The burner’s flame pushes the balloon up like a rocket.
explanation: Archimedes’ principle applies in air: the upthrust equals the weight of the outside air displaced. Heating makes the air inside less dense, so the total weight of balloon, basket and hot air becomes less than the upthrust and the balloon rises.
hints: What happens to the density of air when it is heated?

subject: Physics
q: A wooden block of volume 0.002 m³ floats in water with 75% of its volume under the surface. What is the mass of the block? (density of water = 1000 kg/m³)
explanation: A floating body displaces its own weight of water. Volume submerged = 0.75 × 0.002 = 0.0015 m³, which holds 0.0015 × 1000 = 1.5 kg of water. So the block’s mass is 1.5 kg (and its density 750 kg/m³).
misconception: 2 kg would be the mass if the block were fully submerged.
hints: A floating object displaces water equal to its own weight.
How much water does the submerged part displace?

subject: Physics
q: A runner completes exactly one lap of a 400 m circular track in 80 s. What are her average speed and average velocity for the lap?
explanation: Average speed = total distance ÷ time = 400 m ÷ 80 s = 5 m/s. Average velocity = displacement ÷ time; after one full lap she is back at the start, so displacement = 0 and average velocity = 0.
misconception: Speed and velocity are not interchangeable: velocity uses displacement (with direction), which is zero for a closed loop.
hints: Where does she finish compared with where she started?
Velocity uses displacement, speed uses distance.

subject: Physics
q: A car starts from rest, accelerates uniformly and covers 100 m in the first 10 s. What is its speed at the end of the 10 s?
explanation: s = ½at² gives 100 = ½ × a × 100, so a = 2 m/s². Then v = at = 2 × 10 = 20 m/s. Shortcut: for uniform acceleration from rest, average speed = v/2, so v = 2 × (100/10) = 20 m/s.
misconception: 10 m/s is the AVERAGE speed. Because the car started from rest, its final speed is twice the average.
hints: Use s = ut + ½at² with u = 0.
Average speed for uniform acceleration = (u + v)/2.

subject: Physics
q: A cyclist’s velocity was recorded every 2 s (the velocity changes uniformly between readings). What is the total displacement in the 6 s?
explanation: Displacement = area under the velocity–time graph. 0–2 s: triangle ½ × 2 × 8 = 8 m; 2–4 s: rectangle 2 × 8 = 16 m; 4–6 s: triangle 8 m. Total = 32 m.
misconception: 48 m comes from treating the velocity as 8 m/s for the whole 6 s; the speeding-up and slowing-down phases only count half.
hints: Sketch the v–t graph: it is a trapezium.
Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height.

subject: Physics
q: A stone dropped from rest from the top of a tower travels 25 m during the LAST second before it hits the ground. How tall is the tower? (g = 10 m/s², ignore air resistance)
explanation: If the fall lasts T seconds, distance in the last second = ½g[T² − (T − 1)²] = 5(2T − 1). Setting 5(2T − 1) = 25 gives T = 3 s. Height = ½ × 10 × 3² = 45 m. Check: in 2 s it falls 20 m, so the last second covers 45 − 20 = 25 m ✓.
misconception: Assuming the stone moves at a steady 25 m/s or that the last-second distance equals the height ignores that it keeps accelerating.
hints: Let the total fall time be T. Write the distance fallen in T seconds and in (T − 1) seconds.
The difference of the two distances is 25 m: 5T² − 5(T − 1)² = 25.

subject: Physics
q: Train A (150 m long, 20 m/s) and train B (100 m long, 30 m/s) move towards each other on parallel tracks. How long do they take to pass each other completely, from fronts meeting to rears separating?
explanation: Relative speed for opposite directions = 20 + 30 = 50 m/s. To pass completely, the relative distance covered must equal the sum of the lengths, 250 m. Time = 250 ÷ 50 = 5 s.
misconception: 25 s uses the relative speed for trains moving in the SAME direction (30 − 20 = 10 m/s).
hints: Imagine sitting on train A: how fast does B approach you?
The distance to cover is the total length of both trains.

subject: Physics
q: A car goes round a circular roundabout at a constant speed of 30 km/h. Which statement is correct?
options: Its acceleration is along its direction of motion.
It is accelerating only if its speed increases.
Its velocity changes because its direction changes, so it is accelerating.
Its velocity is constant, so it is not accelerating.
explanation: Velocity is a vector. In circular motion the direction keeps changing, so velocity changes and the car accelerates even at constant speed. This (centripetal) acceleration points towards the centre of the circle, perpendicular to the motion.
misconception: Acceleration is not just “speeding up”; any change of velocity — including a change of direction — is acceleration.
hints: Is velocity a scalar or a vector?

subject: Physics
q: A car travelling at 72 km/h brakes with uniform deceleration and stops in 4 s. How far does it travel while braking?
explanation: 72 km/h = 72 × 1000/3600 = 20 m/s. With uniform deceleration, average speed = (20 + 0)/2 = 10 m/s. Distance = 10 × 4 = 40 m.
misconception: 144 m comes from using 72 directly without converting km/h to m/s; 80 m forgets that the speed falls to zero.
hints: Convert km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6.
Average speed = (initial + final)/2 for uniform deceleration.

subject: Physics
q: A car braking at 36 km/h stops in 10 m. If the driver brakes with exactly the same deceleration from 72 km/h, what is the braking distance?
explanation: From v² = u² + 2as with v = 0: s = u²/(2a). For the same deceleration, s ∝ u². Doubling the speed multiplies the braking distance by 2² = 4, so 10 m × 4 = 40 m. This is why speed limits matter so much near schools.
misconception: Doubling speed does not double braking distance — kinetic energy (and so the braking distance) grows with the SQUARE of speed.
hints: Which equation links speed and distance without time?
With v = 0, s = u²/2a. What happens to u²?

subject: Physics
q: What does the slope of a distance–time graph represent?
explanation: Slope = change in distance ÷ change in time = speed. A steeper line means a faster object; a horizontal line means the object is at rest. (The slope of a velocity–time graph gives acceleration.)
misconception: Students often mix this up with the velocity–time graph, whose slope is acceleration and whose area is displacement.
hints: Slope = rise ÷ run. What is distance ÷ time?

subject: Physics
q:
Consider the statements:
I. A body can have zero velocity and a non-zero acceleration at the same instant.
II. A body moving at constant speed cannot be accelerating.
III. Acceleration is always in the direction of motion.
Which are correct?
explanation: I is true: a ball thrown upward has v = 0 at the top but a = g downward. II is false: uniform circular motion has constant speed but is accelerated. III is false: a braking car accelerates opposite to its motion, and in circular motion acceleration is perpendicular to motion.
misconception: It is tempting to think “stopped” means “no acceleration”, but acceleration depends on how velocity is changing, not on its current value.
hints: Think of a ball at the very top of its flight.
Think of a car going round a bend at steady speed.

subject: Physics
q: A standing passenger falls backwards when a stationary bus starts suddenly. This is best explained by:
options: friction from the floor pushing backwards
explanation: The bus floor drags the passenger’s feet forward, but the upper body tends to stay at rest because of inertia (Newton’s first law). The body therefore appears to fall backwards relative to the bus.
misconception: No backward force pushes the passenger; the upper body simply resists the change from rest.
hints: Which part of the body is pulled forward by the bus, and which is not?

subject: Physics
q: A 150 g cricket ball moving at 20 m/s is caught and brought to rest in 0.1 s. What is the average force exerted by the fielder’s hands?
explanation: Change in momentum = m × v = 0.15 kg × 20 m/s = 3 kg m/s. Average force = Δp/Δt = 3/0.1 = 30 N.
misconception: 300 N comes from using 150 instead of 0.15 kg and dividing wrongly; always convert grams to kilograms.
hints: Force = change in momentum ÷ time.
Convert 150 g to kg first.

subject: Physics
q: A fielder pulls his hands back while catching a fast cricket ball. Why does this reduce the sting?
options: It increases the time over which the momentum changes, reducing the force.
It reduces the ball’s change in momentum.
It reduces the mass of the ball relative to the hands.
It converts the ball’s momentum into heat.
explanation: The ball must lose all its momentum either way (Δp is fixed). Since F = Δp/Δt, spreading the stop over a longer time Δt reduces the average force on the hands. Airbags, crumple zones and sand pits for long jumpers use the same idea.
misconception: The momentum change is the same whether or not the hands move back — only the time, and therefore the force, changes.
hints: Is the ball’s total change in momentum different?
F = Δp ÷ Δt.

subject: Physics
q: A 20 g bullet leaves a 5 kg rifle at 500 m/s. With what speed does the rifle recoil?
explanation: Momentum before firing = 0, so after firing the momenta are equal and opposite: 0.02 × 500 = 5 × v → v = 10/5 = 2 m/s, backwards.
misconception: Using 20 instead of 0.02 kg gives a huge recoil — always convert mass to kilograms.
hints: Total momentum before firing is zero.
m_bullet × v_bullet = m_rifle × v_rifle.

subject: Physics
q: Blocks of 3 kg and 2 kg touch each other on a frictionless floor. A 10 N horizontal push is applied to the 3 kg block, so both move together. What force does the 3 kg block exert on the 2 kg block?
explanation: Acceleration of the pair = 10 N ÷ 5 kg = 2 m/s². The only horizontal force on the 2 kg block is the push from the 3 kg block, which must give it 2 m/s²: F = 2 × 2 = 4 N. (The 3 kg block feels 10 N forward and 4 N backward: net 6 N = 3 × 2 ✓.)
misconception: The full 10 N is not passed on: part of it is needed to accelerate the 3 kg block itself.
hints: First find the common acceleration of both blocks.
Now apply F = ma to the 2 kg block alone.

subject: Physics
q:
Assertion (A): A person standing on a weighing scale in a lift reads more than their true weight while the lift accelerates upward.
Reason (R): To accelerate the person upward, the normal force from the scale must be greater than the person’s weight.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
explanation: Net upward force = N − mg = ma, so N = m(g + a) > mg. The scale reads the normal force N, so it shows more than the true weight. R is exactly the reason for A.
misconception: The scale does not measure mass or gravity directly — it measures the push it must give you.
hints: Write Newton’s second law for the person: which two forces act?

subject: Physics
q: An 80 kg astronaut floating at rest outside a space station throws a 2 kg wrench away at 4 m/s. What happens to the astronaut?
options: Moves at 4 m/s in the opposite direction
Moves at 0.1 m/s in the opposite direction
Stays still, because there is no air to push against
Moves at 0.1 m/s in the same direction as the wrench
explanation: Total momentum starts at zero and is conserved (no external force). 2 × 4 = 80 × v gives v = 0.1 m/s, opposite to the wrench. Rockets work the same way — they need no air to push on.
misconception: Propulsion does not need air. The thrown object pushes back on the thrower (Newton’s third law), in a vacuum too.
hints: Is any external force acting on astronaut + wrench?
Momentum before = momentum after = 0.

subject: Physics
q: Why do action and reaction forces never cancel each other out?
options: They act in the same direction.
Reaction is always slightly smaller than action.
explanation: Newton’s third-law forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, but each acts on a DIFFERENT body. Forces can only cancel if they act on the same body.
misconception: Equal and opposite does not mean balanced: balanced forces must act on the same object.
hints: When you push a wall, which object feels your push and which feels the wall’s push?

subject: Physics
q: A horse pulls a cart. By Newton’s third law the cart pulls back on the horse with an equal force. Why, then, can the horse–cart system accelerate forward?
options: Because the cart’s mass is smaller than the horse’s.
Because the horse’s pull is slightly larger than the cart’s pull.
Because action and reaction cancel, leaving no force.
Because the ground pushes the horse forward (friction) more than the ground’s friction holds the cart back.
explanation: The pull of horse on cart and cart on horse are internal to the system and always equal. The system accelerates because of EXTERNAL forces: the horse pushes the ground backwards, so the ground pushes the horse forwards. If that forward friction exceeds the rolling resistance on the cart, the system accelerates.
misconception: The third-law pair (horse ↔ cart) never decides whether the system moves; only external forces do.
hints: Draw the forces on the horse alone. Which force points forward?

subject: Physics
q: A 5 kg box is pushed along the floor with a horizontal force of 30 N while friction opposes it with 10 N. What is its acceleration?
explanation: Net force = 30 − 10 = 20 N. a = F/m = 20/5 = 4 m/s².
misconception: 6 m/s² ignores friction; Newton’s second law uses the NET force.
hints: Find the net force first.

subject: Physics
q: In a crash, a passenger’s 5 kg head moving at 15 m/s is stopped by an airbag in 0.1 s instead of by the dashboard in 0.01 s. What is the average force on the head with the airbag?
explanation: Δp = 5 × 15 = 75 kg m/s in both cases. With the airbag F = 75/0.1 = 750 N; with the dashboard F = 75/0.01 = 7500 N. Increasing the stopping time tenfold reduces the force tenfold — the physics behind car safety design.
misconception: 7500 N is the dashboard force. The airbag does not change the momentum lost, only the time taken.
hints: Momentum change is the same in both cases.
F = Δp/Δt with Δt = 0.1 s.

subject: Physics
q: An astronaut has a mass of 60 kg on Earth. What is her mass on the Moon, where gravity is about one-sixth as strong?
explanation: Mass is the amount of matter and does not change with location. Her WEIGHT on the Moon is about one-sixth of her weight on Earth (≈ 98 N instead of ≈ 588 N), but her mass stays 60 kg.
misconception: Mass and weight are different quantities: weight is a force (N) that depends on g; mass (kg) does not.
hints: Does the amount of matter in her body change?

subject: Physics
q: The gravitational force between two bodies is F. If the mass of one body is doubled and the distance between them is halved, the new force is:
explanation: F ∝ m₁m₂/r². Doubling one mass multiplies F by 2; halving r multiplies F by 1/(½)² = 4. New force = 2 × 4 × F = 8F.
misconception: Halving the distance quadruples the force (inverse SQUARE), not doubles it.
hints: Treat each change separately and multiply the factors.

subject: Physics
q: A newly discovered planet has the same average density as Earth but twice Earth’s radius. What is the acceleration due to gravity on its surface? (g on Earth = 9.8 m/s²)
explanation: g = GM/R² and M = ρ × (4/3)πR³, so g = (4/3)πGρR — proportional to R for a fixed density. Doubling R doubles g: 2 × 9.8 = 19.6 m/s². (The mass becomes 8 times larger, but the radius-squared term divides by 4.)
misconception: 4.9 m/s² assumes the mass stays the same while the radius doubles; but at the same density, a bigger planet has much more mass.
hints: Write the planet’s mass in terms of density and radius.
Substitute into g = GM/R² — what power of R remains?

subject: Physics
q: A feather and a coin are released together inside a long tube from which all the air has been pumped out. What is observed?
explanation: Without air resistance, every object near Earth’s surface falls with the same acceleration g, whatever its mass. In air the feather falls slowly only because air resistance is large compared with its tiny weight.
misconception: Heavier objects do not fall faster: a larger mass has a proportionally larger weight, so a = W/m = g is the same.
hints: What slows the feather down in ordinary air?

subject: Physics
q: At what height above Earth’s surface does the acceleration due to gravity fall to one-quarter of its surface value? (Earth’s radius ≈ 6400 km)
explanation: g ∝ 1/r², where r is distance from Earth’s CENTRE. For g to become g/4, r must double: r = 2R. Height above the surface = 2R − R = R = 6400 km.
misconception: 12,800 km is the distance from the centre, not the height above the surface.
hints: Gravity depends on distance from the centre of the Earth.
For ¼ of g, by what factor must that distance grow?

subject: Physics
q:
Consider:
I. Your weight can change from place to place on Earth.
II. g is slightly greater at the poles than at the equator.
III. The universal gravitational constant G decreases with altitude.
Which are correct?
explanation: I: weight = mg and g varies, so weight varies. II: Earth is slightly flattened and spinning, so g ≈ 9.83 m/s² at the poles vs ≈ 9.78 m/s² at the equator. III: G is a universal constant (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²); it is g, not G, that changes.
misconception: Mixing up g (local, variable) and G (universal constant) is one of the most common errors in gravitation.
hints: Which symbol is a universal constant: g or G?

subject: Physics
q: A simple pendulum of fixed length is taken to a planet where the acceleration due to gravity is four times that on Earth. What happens to its time period?
options: It stays the same, because the length is unchanged.
explanation: T = 2π√(L/g). With g four times larger, √(1/4) = ½, so the period halves: the pendulum swings faster because the stronger gravity pulls it back more quickly.
misconception: The period depends on the square ROOT of g, not on g directly, so ×4 gravity gives ½ the period, not ¼.
hints: Recall T = 2π√(L/g).
What is √(1/4)?

subject: Physics
q: A stone is dropped from rest from a cliff 80 m high. How long does it take to reach the ground? (g = 10 m/s², ignore air resistance)
explanation: h = ½gt² → 80 = 5t² → t² = 16 → t = 4 s.
misconception: 8 s comes from forgetting the ½ in h = ½gt²; 16 s forgets to take the square root.
hints: Use h = ½gt².

subject: Physics
q: Why does a sharp knife cut vegetables more easily than a blunt one, for the same push?
options: The sharp edge has a larger area, so the force is greater.
A sharp knife has less friction, so the force is greater.
The sharp edge has a smaller area, so the pressure is greater.
explanation: Pressure = force ÷ area. The same force acting on the tiny area of a sharp edge produces a much greater pressure, enough to break the vegetable’s cells.
misconception: Sharpening does not change the force you apply — it changes the area over which it acts.
hints: Pressure = force ÷ area. Which changes when a knife is sharpened?

subject: Physics
q: A 2 kg brick rests on a table on its face measuring 10 cm × 20 cm. What pressure does it exert on the table? (g = 10 m/s²)
explanation: Weight = 2 × 10 = 20 N. Area = 0.1 m × 0.2 m = 0.02 m². Pressure = 20/0.02 = 1000 Pa.
misconception: Using 200 cm² without converting to m² gives 0.1 — areas must be in m² for pascals (1 m² = 10,000 cm²).
hints: Find the weight (force) first.
Convert cm to m before multiplying.

subject: Physics
q: Ice (density 900 kg/m³) floats in fresh water (1000 kg/m³). What percentage of an ice cube’s volume is above the water surface?
explanation: For a floating body, fraction submerged = ρ_body/ρ_liquid = 900/1000 = 0.9, i.e. 90% under water. So 10% is above the surface — the origin of “the tip of the iceberg”.
misconception: 90% is the fraction BELOW the surface.
hints: Fraction submerged = density of body ÷ density of liquid.

subject: Physics
q: A glass is filled to the brim with water with an ice cube floating in it. The ice cube melts completely. What happens?
options: The water level stays exactly at the brim.
It depends on the room temperature.
explanation: A floating ice cube displaces its own WEIGHT of water. When it melts, it becomes water of exactly that weight, which occupies exactly the volume it was already displacing. So the level does not change. (Melting LAND ice, which is not floating, does raise sea level.)
misconception: The part of the ice above water seems as if it should overflow, but ice is less dense than water — it shrinks to fill exactly the “hole” it made.
hints: How much water does a floating object displace — its volume or its weight?
What weight of water does the cube become when it melts?

subject: Physics
q: A metal object weighs 10 N in air and 6 N when fully submerged in water (density 1000 kg/m³). What is the density of the metal?
explanation: Buoyant force = 10 − 6 = 4 N = weight of water displaced. Relative density = weight in air ÷ loss of weight in water = 10/4 = 2.5, so density = 2500 kg/m³.
misconception: 1667 kg/m³ comes from dividing by the apparent weight (6 N) instead of by the LOSS of weight (4 N).
hints: The loss of weight equals the buoyant force.
Relative density = weight in air ÷ loss of weight in water.

subject: Physics
q: An egg sinks in a glass of tap water but floats after enough salt is dissolved. What is the best explanation?
options: Salt dissolves the egg shell, making it hollow.
Salt reduces the surface tension of water.
Salt water is denser, so the same displaced volume weighs more and gives a larger upthrust.
explanation: Upthrust = volume displaced × density of liquid × g. Dissolving salt raises the density of the water. Once the liquid is denser than the egg, the upthrust on the fully submerged egg exceeds its weight and it rises until it floats.
misconception: The egg’s weight does not change. An object floats or sinks depending on its density compared with the LIQUID’s density.
hints: Which changes: the egg or the liquid?
Upthrust depends on the density of the liquid.

subject: Physics
q: A boat carrying a heavy iron anchor floats in a swimming pool. The anchor is thrown overboard and sinks to the bottom. What happens to the water level in the pool?
options: It rises, then returns to the original level.
explanation: In the boat, the anchor is floating indirectly, so it displaces water equal to its WEIGHT. Iron is about 8 times denser than water, so that is a large volume. On the bottom it displaces only its own VOLUME, which is much smaller. Less water is displaced, so the level falls.
misconception: Many expect no change because “the same things are in the pool”. What matters is how much water is displaced: weight-equivalent when floating, volume-equivalent when sunk.
hints: How much water does the anchor displace while it rides in the boat?
How much does it displace lying on the bottom? Compare, given iron is denser than water.

subject: Physics
q: What is the pressure due to water alone at a depth of 10 m in a lake? (density of water 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s²)
explanation: P = hρg = 10 × 1000 × 10 = 100,000 Pa = 1 × 10⁵ Pa — roughly the same as atmospheric pressure. So a diver at 10 m feels about twice the pressure at the surface.
misconception: Pressure in a liquid depends on depth, not on the size or shape of the lake.
hints: Use P = hρg.

subject: Physics
q: How much work does Earth’s gravity do on a satellite moving in a perfectly circular orbit during one revolution?
options: Positive, because gravity pulls the satellite
Zero, because the force is always perpendicular to the displacement
mgh, where h is the height of the orbit
Negative, because the satellite moves away from Earth
explanation: W = Fs cos θ. In a circular orbit, gravity points to the centre while the motion is tangential, so θ = 90° and cos 90° = 0 at every instant. No work is done, which is why the satellite’s speed stays constant.
misconception: A force can act continuously yet do no work if it is perpendicular to the motion.
hints: What is the angle between gravity and the satellite’s velocity?

subject: Physics
q: A 1000 kg car speeds up from 10 m/s to 20 m/s. How much work must the net force do on it?
explanation: Work–energy theorem: W = ΔKE = ½m(v² − u²) = ½ × 1000 × (400 − 100) = 150,000 J = 150 kJ.
misconception: 50 kJ uses ½m(v − u)², squaring the change in speed instead of taking the change in v².
hints: Work done = change in kinetic energy.
Compute KE at each speed separately.

subject: Physics
q: A motor lifts a 200 kg load through a height of 15 m in 30 s at steady speed. What is the power output of the motor? (g = 10 m/s²)
misconception: Forgetting g (using mass instead of weight) gives 100 W.
hints: Work done against gravity = mgh.
Power = work ÷ time.

subject: Physics
q: A pendulum bob is pulled aside until it is 45 cm higher than its lowest point and then released. Ignoring air resistance, how fast is it moving as it passes through the lowest point? (g = 10 m/s²)
explanation: Energy conservation: mgh = ½mv², so v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 10 × 0.45) = √9 = 3 m/s. The mass cancels, and the length of the string does not matter — only the drop in height.
misconception: You do not need the length of the string or the mass of the bob: only the vertical height drop matters.
hints: Which energy changes into which?
Set mgh = ½mv² and solve for v (h in metres).

subject: Physics
q: A pump that is 75% efficient lifts 300 kg of water into a tank 20 m above the ground. How much electrical energy does it use? (g = 10 m/s²)
explanation: Useful work = mgh = 300 × 10 × 20 = 60,000 J. Efficiency = useful output/input, so input = 60,000/0.75 = 80,000 J = 80 kJ. The extra 20 kJ is wasted, mostly as heat and sound.
misconception: 45 kJ multiplies by 0.75 instead of dividing: the input must always be LARGER than the useful output.
hints: Find the useful energy first.
Input energy = useful energy ÷ efficiency.

subject: Physics
q:
Assertion (A): A person holding a heavy suitcase while standing still does no work on the suitcase.
Reason (R): Work done is zero when the displacement is zero.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A.
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
explanation: W = Fs cos θ; with s = 0, W = 0 regardless of the force. The person still gets tired because muscles use chemical energy internally, but no mechanical work is done on the suitcase.
misconception: Feeling tired is not evidence of mechanical work.
hints: Does the suitcase move?

subject: Physics
q: Astronauts on a spacewalk cannot hear each other directly even when shouting close by. Why?
options: Sound needs a material medium, and space is almost a vacuum.
Sound is too slow in space.
explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave — vibrations passed from particle to particle. In the near-vacuum of space there are almost no particles, so sound cannot travel. Astronauts use radio (an electromagnetic wave), which does not need a medium.
misconception: Light and radio cross a vacuum because they are electromagnetic waves; sound cannot.
hints: What does sound travel through?

subject: Physics
q: A sound wave has a frequency of 500 Hz and a wavelength of 0.68 m. What is its speed?
explanation: v = fλ = 500 × 0.68 = 340 m/s, the speed of sound in air at about 20 °C.
misconception: Dividing f by λ instead of multiplying gives a meaningless 735.
hints: Use v = f × λ.

subject: Physics
q: The sensation of a sound persists in our brain for about 0.1 s. What is the minimum distance from a reflecting wall for a distinct echo to be heard, if the speed of sound is 344 m/s?
explanation: For a distinct echo, the reflected sound must arrive at least 0.1 s after the original. In 0.1 s sound travels 34.4 m — but that is the round trip, there and back. So the wall must be at least 34.4/2 = 17.2 m away.
misconception: 34.4 m forgets that the sound has to travel to the wall AND back.
hints: How far does sound go in 0.1 s?
An echo is a round trip.

subject: Physics
q: A sound wave passes from air into water, where sound travels about four times faster. Which describes the wave in water?
explanation: Frequency is set by the source and does not change when a wave crosses into a new medium (every incoming vibration produces one vibration on the other side). Since v = fλ and v increases about 4 times, λ increases about 4 times.
misconception: Pitch (frequency) does not change at a boundary — the wavelength changes instead.
hints: What decides frequency: the source or the medium?
Then use v = fλ.

subject: Physics
q: A ship’s SONAR sends an ultrasonic pulse straight down. The echo from the seabed returns after 2 s. If sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water, how deep is the sea?
explanation: Total path = 1500 × 2 = 3000 m, which is down and back up. Depth = 3000/2 = 1500 m.
misconception: 3000 m forgets that the pulse travels the depth twice.
hints: Distance = speed × time — but for which journey?

subject: Physics
q: Putting your ear to a railway line, you can hear an approaching train before you hear it through the air. Why?
options: Sound travels faster in steel than in air.
Sound travels in straight lines only through solids.
